content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition associated with significant illness and mortality, which worsens as the disease progresses to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). There is growing interest in developing innovative, effective, and cost-efficient strategies to engage patients, improve health behaviors, and enhance clinical outcomes. Globally, the use of technology has increased dramatically, and eHealth interventions are being explored as a means to improve access to health information, enhance healthcare quality, and promote healthier behaviors among patients. This review aimed to assess the potential benefits and harms of eHealth interventions in modifying health behaviors in individuals with CKD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to January 14, 2019. The search included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that utilized eHealth interventions to promote behavior change in CKD patients were included, with no restrictions on outcomes, language, or publication type. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The certainty of the evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. A total of 43 studies involving 6,617 participants were included in the review. These studies varied widely in terms of the eHealth modalities used, the type of intervention, the CKD population studied, and the outcomes assessed. Most studies (39 out of 43) were conducted in adult populations, with 16 studies focusing on patients undergoing dialysis, 11 studies on pre-dialysis patients, 15 studies on kidney transplant recipients, and 1 study on transplant candidates. Six different eHealth modalities were identified: telehealth, mobile or tablet applications, text or email messaging, electronic monitoring devices, internet-based platforms or websites, and video or DVD-based interventions. Three studies employed a combination of these modalities. The interventions were categorized into six types: educational interventions, reminder systems, self-monitoring tools, behavioral counseling, clinical decision aids, and mixed intervention types. The review identified 98 outcomes, which were grouped into nine domains: blood pressure (9 studies), biochemical parameters (6 studies), clinical endpoints (16 studies), dietary intake (3 studies), quality of life (9 studies), medication adherence (10 studies), behavior (7 studies), physical activity (1 study), and cost-effectiveness (7 studies). However, only three outcomes could be meta-analyzed due to significant heterogeneity in the study populations and eHealth modalities used. The meta-analysis revealed a reduction in interdialytic weight gain by 0.13 kg (4 studies, 335 participants; mean difference [MD] -0.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.28 to 0.01; I² = 0%) and a reduction in dietary sodium intake by 197 mg/day (2 studies, 181 participants; MD -197, 95% CI -540.7 to 146.8; I² = 0%). However, the evidence for these outcomes was graded as low quality due to high or unclear risk of bias, indirectness (for interdialytic weight gain), and imprecision (for dietary sodium intake). Three studies reported mortality outcomes, involving 2,799 participants and 146 deaths. The mortality rate was 45 deaths per 1,000 cases in the eHealth intervention group compared to 61 deaths per 1,000 cases in the standard care group (relative risk [RR] 0.74, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.03; P = 0.08). However, the certainty of this evidence was also graded as low due to high or unclear risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision. Therefore, it remains uncertain whether eHealth interventions, when added to usual care, have a significant impact on mortality rates. In conclusion, eHealth interventions may offer some benefits in managing dietary sodium intake and fluid management in CKD patients. However, the overall quality of evidence supporting the use of eHealth interventions in this population is low. The findings are limited by methodological weaknesses, variability in eHealth modalities, and differences in intervention types. This review underscores the need for high-quality, robust research that includes a standardized core dataset to facilitate meaningful evaluation and comparison of the evidence.
